You understand and use the modal particles that give speech its tone: Komm doch mit! Das ist ja toll! Mach mal Pause. Das ist eben so. Was ist denn los? Das wird schon klappen.
to go well, to work out
Could you help me for a moment?
Recognise modal particles and understand what emotion they add (insistence, surprise, reassurance, resignation).
Use “mal” and “doch” in requests and invitations (Komm doch mal vorbei!).
Use “denn” and “eigentlich” in relaxed questions (Wo wohnst du eigentlich?).
Know where they go in the sentence (usually after the verb and pronouns, before the rest).

It's December 2033. Mara and Jakob are planning their wedding for May 2034. Mara's mother wants an Orthodox wedding in Sibiu, Jakob's mother wants the Protestant church in their village in Thuringia. Mara and Jakob argue, with lots of particles.
Jakob, come on, say something! Mum has already called me three times today.
What should I say? Your mum simply wants an Orthodox wedding in Sibiu. And my mum wants the little church in Thuringia, that's just how it is. It's hardly anything new, is it?
But we live in Berlin, after all! Our friends are here. Ludwig is here. He can't exactly fly to Sibiu at eighty-five.
That's true. And Grete and Friedrich even less so.
Exactly! So what are we going to do? We can't get married three times, can we?
Excuse me? You must be mad!

No, listen. In May, the registry office here in Berlin, with everyone from the house. In July, the Orthodox church in Sibiu, for your family. And in August a party in Thuringia, in my mum's garden. No second wedding, just a party.
That's crazy. That's… actually not a bad idea at all.
See. I do have good ideas sometimes. Not often, but sometimes.
Oh, it'll work out. Andrei bakes the cake, Lena takes care of the café, and your dad brings honey. We don't need any more than that, do we?
Just don't you dare call my mum before I've talked to her!
Modal particles are NOT stressed: “Komm doch MIT!” (the stress is on the verb, not on “doch”).

Small, unstressed words that don't change the information, but the TONE: surprise, insistence, reassurance, irritation. Without them, spoken German sounds cold and textbook-like. English expresses this through intonation or with words like “just”, “come on”, “well”, “after all”, “oh well”.
Das weißt du doch! / Komm doch!
Schau mal! Kannst du mal helfen?
Das ist eben so. / Dann gehen wir halt zu Fuß.
moving to another topic, relaxed tone
“halt” is more colloquial and more common in the south; “eben” is more neutral. The meaning is the same.
Particles usually go in the middle of the sentence: after the verb and after unstressed pronouns, before the new information.
Could you pass me the salt?
Several particles can go together, in a fixed order: “ja doch”, “doch mal”, “denn eigentlich”: “Komm doch mal vorbei!” = Do drop by sometime!
Don't put the particle at the beginning of the sentence: “Doch komm mit!” ✗. And don't stress it: a stressed “DOCH” means something else (Yes, it is! / Oh yes!).
Many particles are also ordinary words, with their own meaning:
Doch ich habe es dir gesagt.
Ich habe es dir doch gesagt.
Ich habe doch es dir gesagt.
Wo will Maras Mutter die Hochzeit?
in einer orthodoxen Kirche in Sibiu
Standesamt in Berlin, Kirche in Sibiu, Fest in Thüringen
Warum kann Ludwig nicht nach Sibiu fliegen?

The Christmas recital at the “Am Kollwitzpark” care home took place on the third Sunday of Advent, on a Sunday afternoon when it was snowing outside for the first time that winter. The common room was decorated with fir twigs and straw stars that the residents had made in the craft group, and on every table there was a plate of biscuits baked by Andrei: vanilla crescents, cinnamon stars and, at Grete's special request, Spekulatius. Ayşe Yilmaz was sitting in the front row and was so pale that Mara took her pulse twice. “You're frozen stiff,” she said. “Do have some tea.”

Ludwig was sitting next to Friedrich by the window, in his good Sunday suit, quietly telling him about the wedding plans that Mara and Jakob had presented in his living room the evening before. The registry office in May, the church in Sibiu in July, the party in Thuringia in August. “Three weddings,” Ludwig said, shaking his head. “I married Ingrid once, on a Tuesday, in twenty minutes, and afterwards we had sausages.” Friedrich laughed softly. “And was it beautiful?” Ludwig thought about it. “It was the most beautiful Tuesday of my life,” he said. “But I'm not telling Mara that. Otherwise she'll want a fourth one too.”

It was Ayşe's first recital. Her very first, at forty-one. She had practised every evening for three months, on the black piano in the living room, after the children were in bed, with the mute pedal, so the neighbours wouldn't complain. Her husband had said she was overdoing it. Her elder daughter had said she should just play, it was only an old people's home after all. And Grete had said: “In music there is no «only». An audience is an audience. Even if it consists of twelve old people who sleep through half the concert.”

Elif played first. She played two little pieces from Schumann's “Album for the Young”, without mistakes, with a straight back and a serious face, as Grete had taught her. When she had finished, she bowed, exactly as deeply as Grete had shown her, not too deep, not too shallow, and the residents applauded, even those who had just woken up. Mr Petrowski from room 14, who hadn't said a word for three years, clapped the loudest. The carer sitting next to him had tears in her eyes.

Grete, who was sitting in her armchair next to the piano, had been tapping the beat on her knee with her pencil the whole time, barely audibly. When Elif had finished, she said nothing, but she put the pencil down. Mara, who knew Grete well by now, knew what that meant: there was nothing to correct. Elif knew too. She was beaming so much that she almost forgot to go back to her seat, and Ludwig had to signal to her.

Then it was Ayşe's turn. She stood up, went to the piano, sat down, and then the thing she had been afraid of for three months happened: her mind went blank. Completely blank. She looked at the keys and no longer knew how the piece began. The seconds passed. Five. Ten. Someone coughed. Ayşe felt the blood rising to her cheeks and thought: now I'll get up and leave. I'm simply not a pianist. I'm a cashier from Kayseri who started too late.

And then she heard a soft sound. Tick. Tock. Tick. Tock. She turned her head. Grete had put an old wooden metronome on the piano, one with a small silver pendulum, and had set it going. Tick. Tock. Slowly, calmly, like a heartbeat. Grete said nothing. She just looked at Ayşe, with her clear, ironic gaze, and nodded once. And Ayşe listened to the ticking, breathed, put her hands on the keys and suddenly knew again how the piece began. Her fingers knew. They had known all along.

She played “Of Foreign Lands and Peoples”. Not perfectly. In the third line she played too fast again, and once she hit a wrong note. But she played to the end, and when the last note had faded, there was a moment of complete silence in the room. Then Mr Petrowski from room 14 stood up, slowly, leaning on his walking frame, and said in a hoarse, unused voice that nobody had heard for three years: “Lovely. That really was lovely.” The carer dropped her cup in surprise.

Then everyone applauded, louder than for Elif, and Ayşe stayed sitting at the piano for a while, with her hands in her lap, and couldn't get up. Her knees were trembling. Mara came over and helped her up, and on the way back to her seat Ayşe whispered: “I made a mistake. In the third line.” Mara laughed. “Nobody noticed, really,” she said. “Except Mrs Hoffmann. And she only helped you.” Ayşe looked at Grete, who was already talking to Friedrich again as if nothing had happened, and thought that she would never forget this woman, even if she lived to be a hundred.

After the recital, when the biscuits had been eaten and most of the guests had left, Grete called Elif over. She took the old metronome from the piano and gave it to her. “It belonged to my first teacher,” she said. “Mr Wendland. He gave it to me in 1943, when I was seven, in the cellar, while the bombs were falling outside. He said: when you're afraid, listen to the metronome. It isn't afraid. It simply keeps going.” She closed Elif's little hands around the wood. “It has helped me for ninety years. Now it will help you. And one day you'll pass it on too. That's just how it's done.”
But Mrs Hoffmann, you still need it! You still play, after all!

Child, I'm ninety-seven. I know where the beat is by now. And if I ever forget it, Friedrich is sitting right next to me tapping his foot, isn't he. Far too loudly, by the way. He never had any sense of rhythm.

Friedrich, who was sitting by the window, pretended not to have heard. But he was smiling. In recent weeks he had become more tired, slower. He slept a lot, during the day too, and sometimes, in the middle of a conversation, he forgot what he wanted to say. Mara had noticed. She hadn't told anyone, not even Jakob. But now she dropped by every evening after her shift, as she had promised Grete in February, and brought him the newspaper he no longer read, and stayed ten minutes, sometimes an hour.

That afternoon, as Mara was getting ready to leave, Friedrich held her by the arm. “Mara,” he said quietly, so that Grete wouldn't hear. “You promised her something. In February. I know. She told me.” Mara blushed. “Mr Mertens, I…” He shook his head. “No, listen to me. I just want to tell you: don't worry about me. Worry about her. When I'm gone, she'll be alone. And she'll pretend everything is fine. That's what she always does, after all.” Mara nodded and couldn't say anything. Friedrich let go of her arm and smiled again, as if he had been talking about the weather.

On the way home, through the snow, at the new stop, where Elif's tree now stood bare and wore a thin white cap of snow, Elif held the metronome under her jacket so it wouldn't get wet. Ayşe walked beside her, silent, with red cheeks, still trembling a little. At the corner she suddenly stopped. “Elif,” she said. “What did Mr Petrowski actually say? I didn't quite understand. I was so nervous.” Elif looked at her mother, very seriously, and said: “He said: that really was lovely, Mum. With «ja». Mrs Hoffmann says that when a German says «ja», he really means it.”

Ayşe laughed, then cried a little, then laughed again, in the middle of Kastanienallee, in the snow, and the people waiting at the stop looked at her in surprise. That evening, in the notebook in which she had been writing down new German words for six years, she wrote a single word, with an exclamation mark after it: “ja!” And underneath, in Turkish, the translation, which didn't exist, because for this little German word there is no real translation in any language.

Late that evening, Elif's father came home. He hadn't been able to come to the recital because he had a late shift on the bus, and he had been thinking about his wife all day, at every stop, as he admitted later. He saw the notebook on the kitchen table, with a single word and the exclamation mark, and only asked: “Well?” Ayşe looked up from her tea and said: “I did it. With one mistake. And with a metronome.” Mr Yilmaz laughed, sat down next to her and took her hand, and Elif, who should actually have been in bed long ago, crept into the kitchen in her pyjamas and solemnly placed the old metronome in the middle of the table, where it stayed all night.
Was passierte, als Ayşe am Flügel saß?
